Neuland is part of the Mennonite colony region of the Chaco. The settlement is connected with the history of communities that established farms and built their lives in a dry natural environment. A visit complements time in Filadelfia and the story of the settlers told at the Jakob Unger Museum.

Travelling through the area offers views of local settlements and the surrounding flat landscape. Neuland reveals the cultural side of the Chaco alongside its natural areas and historic sites. It is a part of the route where everyday community life helps explain how people adapted to local conditions.

Neumayer Channel runs between Wiencke Island and the southeastern part of Anvers Island in the Palmer Archipelago. Its general orientation is northeast to southwest. Sailing through the channel offers views of the islands' slopes and glaciers from the water, with changing perspectives gradually revealing new stretches of shoreline.

The southwestern entrance to the channel was sighted by Eduard Dallmann's German expedition in 1873–1874. The Belgian Antarctic Expedition sailed through and charted the channel in February 1898, naming it after Georg von Neumayer, a German geographer and supporter of polar exploration. Passage through the channel remains part of a marine itinerary and depends on ice and weather conditions.

At Nido de Cóndores, the tents stand high above the valleys, surrounded by scree and patches of snow. The Andean ranges stretch away beyond the camp. The air is colder here, movements become slower, and even a short walk to fetch water feels very different from down below. In the evening, settling into a tent with a hot drink and watching the last light leave the mountains is especially welcome.

Nido de Cóndores, or 'Condors' Nest', is one of the high camps on Aconcagua's normal route. It lies above Camp Canadá, at an altitude of more than 5,000 m. Mountaineering expeditions reach this stop after approaching via Plaza de Mulas and completing several acclimatisation outings.

The Ada Tours itinerary includes setting up camp, resting and continuing to adapt to the altitude. The group then heads towards Berlín–Cólera, the next stage before a summit attempt. Participants carry their personal equipment themselves, while porters transport part of the group supplies. Weather and individual wellbeing determine the pace; extra time in the expedition schedule allows this section to be completed without rushing.
